provenance.method: lesson notes written from the NERDC 2025 scheme of work outline; every week keeps its scheme topic and bullets as the teaching spine

topics.title: Revision of sss two work
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to recall crop classification methods.
The students should be able to explain soil types and their characteristics.

Introduction:
Last term we studied various crops and soil types in Agricultural Science. Today we will revise these key topics to strengthen our foundation for this term's work.

Content:
Crop classification involves grouping plants based on their botanical families, economic uses, or life cycles. For example, cereals like maize and rice belong to the Poaceae family. Soil types include sandy, clay, and loamy soils, each with distinct properties affecting water retention and nutrient availability. In Nigeria, sandy soils are common in the North while clay soils dominate parts of the Southeast.

Class activity:
Students will work in groups to classify common Nigerian crops into their botanical families and identify soil types using soil samples from different locations.

Evaluation questions:
1. List three crop classification methods.
2. Differentiate between sandy and clay soils.
3. Explain how soil type affects crop production in Nigeria.
4. Name two crops from the legume family.

Summary:
Today's revision has reinforced our understanding of crop classification and soil types which are fundamental to Agricultural Science.

topics.title: Agricultural ecology
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to define ecosystem and habitat.
The students should be able to explain the components of an ecosystem.

Introduction:
We have previously studied how plants interact with their environment. Today we will explore agricultural ecology in more detail to understand these relationships better.

Content:
An ecosystem is a community of living organisms interacting with their physical environment. A habitat is the natural home of an organism. Agricultural ecosystems include both biotic components (plants, animals, microorganisms) and abiotic components (soil, water, climate). For example, a maize farm in Benue State forms an ecosystem where maize plants interact with insects, soil nutrients, and rainfall patterns.

Class activity:
Students will identify and document different components of the school farm ecosystem, noting biotic and abiotic factors and their interactions.

Evaluation questions:
1. Define ecosystem and habitat.
2. List three biotic components of an agricultural ecosystem.
3. Explain how abiotic factors affect crop production during the harmattan season.
4. Differentiate between natural and agricultural ecosystems.

Summary:
Understanding agricultural ecology helps us manage farm systems more effectively by considering all environmental interactions.

topics.title: Rock formation
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to list the three types of rocks.
The students should be able to explain the process of weathering.

Introduction:
In our previous lessons on soil science, we mentioned that rocks break down to form soil. Today we will study rock formation and weathering processes in detail.

Content:
The three types of rocks are igneous, sedimentary, and metamorphic. Igneous rocks form from cooled magma like granite. Sedimentary rocks form from compressed sediments like sandstone. Metamorphic rocks form from altered existing rocks like marble. Weathering is the breakdown of rocks into smaller particles through physical, chemical, and biological processes. In Nigeria, granite rocks in Jos undergo physical weathering due to temperature changes while limestone in Sokoto undergoes chemical weathering.

Class activity:
Students will collect different rock samples from the school environment and classify them into the three rock types, identifying evidence of weathering.

Evaluation questions:
1. Name the three types of rocks with one example each.
2. Explain the difference between physical and chemical weathering.
3. Describe how weathering contributes to soil formation in Nigeria.
4. Identify which type of rock is most common in your locality.

Summary:
Understanding rock formation and weathering processes helps us appreciate how soil is formed and why different regions have different soil types.

topics.title: Soil science
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to describe soil profile.
The students should be able to explain soil properties.

Introduction:
Last week we learned how rocks weather to form soil. Today we will study soil profile and properties which are essential for determining soil suitability for different crops.

Content:
Soil profile is the vertical section of soil showing different layers called horizons. These include topsoil (A horizon), subsoil (B horizon), and parent material (C horizon). Soil properties include texture (sand, silt, clay), structure, pH, organic matter content, and water holding capacity. For example, loamy soil with good structure is ideal for growing cassava in Nigeria as it retains moisture well while sandy soil is better for crops like carrot that need good drainage.

Class activity:
Students will dig a soil profile pit in the school farm and identify the different horizons, collecting samples from each layer for analysis.

Evaluation questions:
1. Describe the three main horizons of a soil profile.
2. Explain how soil texture affects water retention.
3. Differentiate between soil structure and soil texture.
4. Why is pH an important soil property for crop production?

Summary:
Understanding soil profile and properties helps farmers make informed decisions about crop selection and soil management practices.

topics.title: Soil fertility
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to list essential plant nutrients.
The students should be able to explain nutrient cycles.

Introduction:
After studying soil properties, it's important to understand soil fertility which determines how well plants can grow in a particular soil. Today we will explore essential nutrients and their cycles in soil.

Content:
Essential plant nutrients include macronutrients (nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium, calcium, magnesium, sulfur) and micronutrients (iron, zinc, manganese, copper). Nutrient cycles describe how these elements move through the soil-plant system. The nitrogen cycle involves fixation, nitrification, and denitrification processes. For example, when a farmer applies NPK fertilizer to maize in Kaduna State, the nitrogen is absorbed by plants, and excess may be lost through leaching or denitrification.

Class activity:
Students will design a simple experiment to demonstrate nitrogen fixation using leguminous plants and observe changes in soil nitrogen content over time.

Evaluation questions:
1. List three macronutrients essential for plant growth.
2. Explain the nitrogen cycle with its main processes.
3. Differentiate between macronutrients and micronutrients.
4. How does soil organic matter contribute to soil fertility?

Summary:
Understanding soil fertility and nutrient cycles helps farmers apply fertilizers effectively and maintain productive soils for sustainable agriculture.

topics.title: Land use
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to explain different land use types in Nigeria.
The students should be able to discuss factors affecting land use decisions.

Introduction:
We have studied various aspects of soil and crops. Today we will examine how land is used differently across Nigeria and the factors that influence these decisions.

Content:
Land use types in Nigeria include arable farming, forestry, livestock grazing, fishing, and urban development. Arable farming is predominant in the North with crops like millet and sorghum, while the South has more tree crops like oil palm and cocoa. Factors affecting land use include soil type, climate, population density, economic factors, and government policies. For example, the fertile soils of the Benue Valley make it ideal for large-scale farming of yams and cassava, while the coastal areas are used for fishing and aquaculture.

Class activity:
Students will create a land use map of Nigeria identifying major agricultural regions and the crops commonly grown in each area.

Evaluation questions:
1. List four land use types in Nigeria.
2. Explain how soil type influences land use decisions.
3. Describe the relationship between climate and land use in Nigeria.
4. Why is land use planning important for sustainable agriculture?

Summary:
Understanding land use patterns in Nigeria helps us make better decisions about agricultural production and resource management.

topics.title: Crop classification
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to classify crops based on botanical families.
The students should be able to explain economic uses of different crop families.

Introduction:
Throughout our agricultural studies, we have encountered various crops. Today we will systematically classify these crops based on their botanical families and explore their economic importance.

Content:
Crops can be classified based on botanical families, life cycles, economic uses, or growth habits. Botanical families include Poaceae (cereals like maize, rice, millet), Fabaceae (legumes like cowpea, groundnut), Solanaceae (tomato, pepper), and Asteraceae (sunflower). Economic uses of these crops include food production (cassava, yam), industrial raw materials (cotton, rubber), and medicinal purposes (neem tree). In Nigeria, maize from the Poaceae family is a staple food while rubber from the Euphorbiaceae family is an important cash crop.

Class activity:
Students will collect and identify different crop specimens from the school farm, classifying them into their botanical families and documenting their economic uses.

Evaluation questions:
1. Name four botanical families of crops with examples of each.
2. Differentiate between food crops and cash crops with Nigerian examples.
3. Explain how crop classification helps in agricultural planning.
4. List two crops from the Solanaceae family and their uses.

Summary:
Crop classification provides a systematic way to understand the diversity of plants and their importance in agriculture.

topics.title: Crop husbandry
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to describe the practices of maize cultivation.
The students should be able to explain the husbandry of cassava.

Introduction:
We have studied crop classification and now we will focus on the specific practices involved in cultivating two major Nigerian crops: maize and cassava.

Content:
Maize cultivation involves land preparation, planting, weeding, fertilizer application, pest control, and harvesting. In Nigeria, maize is often intercropped with legumes like cowpea. Cassava husbandry includes stem selection, planting at the right spacing, weed control, and harvesting at 8-12 months. Cassava is often planted in mounds or ridges in the southern parts of Nigeria. Both crops require adequate rainfall but maize is more sensitive to drought. For example, in Kano State, maize is planted at the beginning of the rainy season while cassava can be planted throughout the year in the humid South.

Class activity:
Students will practice maize planting techniques in the school farm, preparing land, spacing seeds, and applying fertilizer according to recommended practices.

Evaluation questions:
1. List the main practices in maize cultivation.
2. Explain the importance of stem selection in cassava production.
3. Differentiate between the planting seasons for maize and cassava in Nigeria.
4. Why is intercropping commonly used with maize cultivation?

Summary:
Understanding crop husbandry practices helps farmers optimize production of maize and cassava which are vital to Nigeria's food security.

topics.title: Weed science
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to classify different types of weeds.
The students should be able to explain weed control methods.

Introduction:
In our previous lessons on crop husbandry, we mentioned weed control as an important practice. Today we will study weeds in detail and explore various control methods used in Nigerian agriculture.

Content:
Weeds are unwanted plants that compete with crops for nutrients, water, and sunlight. They can be classified as grasses (e.g. spear grass), broadleaf weeds (e.g. Sida acuta), or sedges (e.g. Cyperus rotundus). Weed control methods include cultural (crop rotation, clean planting), mechanical (hand weeding, hoeing), chemical (herbicides), and biological (using competitive crops or pests). In Nigeria, hand weeding is common in smallholder farms while herbicides are used in large-scale mechanized farms. For example, glyphosate herbicide is often used before planting maize in the North.

Class activity:
Students will identify common weeds in the school farm, classify them into types, and demonstrate at least two weed control methods.

Evaluation questions:
1. Define weeds and explain why they are harmful to crops.
2. Classify weeds into three types with examples.
3. Explain two cultural methods of weed control.
4. Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of using herbicides for weed control.

Summary:
Effective weed management is crucial for maximizing crop yields and reducing production costs in Nigerian agriculture.

topics.title: Revision and WAEC practice
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to answer WAEC-style questions on Agricultural Science.
The students should be able to identify key concepts from the term's work.

Introduction:
As we approach the end of the term, it's important to revise what we've learned and practice exam questions to prepare for WAEC. Today we will review key topics and work through past questions.

Content:
We will review major topics from this term including agricultural ecology, rock formation, soil science, soil fertility, land use, crop classification, crop husbandry, and weed science. Students will work through past WAEC questions covering these areas, focusing on understanding question requirements and structuring answers appropriately. For example, when answering a question on soil profile, students should clearly describe the horizons and their characteristics with relevant Nigerian examples.

Class activity:
Students will work in groups to answer selected past WAEC questions, then present their answers to the class for discussion and marking.

Evaluation questions:
1. Explain the nitrogen cycle with reference to Nigerian agricultural practices.
2. Describe how soil texture affects crop production in different regions of Nigeria.
3. Compare and contrast the husbandry practices of maize and cassava.
4. Discuss the challenges of weed control in Nigerian agriculture.
5. Evaluate the impact of land use changes on agricultural productivity in Nigeria.

Summary:
Today's revision and practice have prepared us for the WAEC examination by reinforcing key concepts and improving our exam technique.
